issues.item: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Grief Reminders' implies bereavement/loss of a deceased person, which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness unless the child died; that is not the stated trauma type. This item appears trauma-incongruent.

issues.item: Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
issues.explanation: 'Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people' suggests interpersonal danger/assault-related threat. The rest of the profile centers on generalized unsafety and negative self-appraisals rather than fear of dangerous people, making this item poorly matched to the trauma type and the other selected items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
issues.explanation: The profile is built around a child's life-threatening illness, but 'vigilant for dangerous people' implies an interpersonal/assault-type danger focus that is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which otherwise reflects generalized vulnerability and medical trauma. This item appears trauma-incongruent for the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Avoiding hospitals/ambulances/physical examinations is plausible for medical trauma, but it sits awkwardly alongside 'vigilant for dangerous people,' which points to a different threat domain. Within Maladaptive Strategies, these two strategies suggest different trauma contexts that are difficult to explain as one coherent profile.

issues.item: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
issues.explanation: For a trauma centered on a child's life-threatening illness, minimizing that the event 'did not really happen or was not that bad' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which shows marked ongoing threat and strongly negative self-appraisals. Thought suppression and avoidance of medical cues fit, but this item points toward denial/minimization in a way that clashes with the severity and emotional meaning of the other endorsed items.

issues.item: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
issues.explanation: 'I wake during the night to check whether I am safe' suggests a danger-focused nighttime safety-checking pattern centered on the patient's own physical safety. In the context of trauma from a child's severe illness, threat is more plausibly organized around the child's safety/health or medical crises. This item is not impossible, but paired with the absence of child-focused threat content it is clinically mismatched to the trauma context.

vignette: As a pharmacist, Yara had always been drawn to the precision and control of her work. But when her 10-year-old son was diagnosed with leukemia, Yara's world began to unravel. She spent countless hours by his side in the hospital, watching as he underwent round after round of grueling treatment. The beeping of machines, the antiseptic smell, and the sterile white walls all blended together into a nightmare that she couldn't wake up from. As her son slowly recovered, Yara found herself struggling to shake off the feelings of weakness and helplessness that had settled over her. She began to believe that there was something fundamentally wrong with her as a person, that she wasn't strong enough to protect her child from harm. This sense of defective self only intensified when she started thinking about why this had happened to her - was it some kind of punishment? Did she somehow deserve it? The more she dwelled on these questions, the more convinced she became that nothing good could ever happen to her again. These negative appraisals began to seep into every aspect of Yara's life. She started avoiding hospitals and ambulances, unable to bear the sight of them without being transported back to those dark days by her son's bedside. Even the sound of sirens in the distance was enough to send her heart racing. She tried hard not to think about the trauma, but it seemed like every noise, every smell, was a trigger waiting to unleash a flood of memories and emotions. As Yara became more withdrawn, she found it increasingly difficult to relax, even when she knew she was safe. Her mind would start racing, jumping from one worst-case scenario to the next, making it impossible for her to fall asleep or stay asleep. The slightest sound - a creaking floorboard, a rustling of leaves - would send her jolting upright, her heart pounding in her chest. The more Yara struggled with these threats, the more she began to believe that she was indeed weak and defective. She felt like she was walking on eggshells, waiting for the next disaster to strike. And so she suppressed her thoughts, trying not to think about the trauma at all - a strategy that only seemed to make things worse. As time went on, Yara's avoidance behaviors began to take a toll on her relationships and work performance. Her colleagues noticed that she was increasingly distant, always seeming preoccupied and on edge. Patients began to complain that she was curt and dismissive, not the warm and caring pharmacist they had come to trust. And yet, despite these consequences, Yara couldn't seem to break free from the cycle of negative appraisals, threat monitoring, and maladaptive strategies that had taken hold. It wasn't until her son's latest check-up - a routine visit that sent Yara into a tailspin of anxiety - that she realized she needed help. She was exhausted, trapped in a never-ending loop of fear and self-doubt. As she sat in the waiting room, watching as families laughed and chatted together, Yara felt a glimmer of hope. Maybe, just maybe, there was a way out of this darkness - a way to break free from the grip of PTSD and start rebuilding her life. Yara's eyes filled with tears as she thought about what had brought her to this point. She was scared - scared that she would never be able to escape the memories of her son's illness, scared that she would never be able to find peace again. But most of all, she was scared that she would lose herself completely in the process. As she stood up, smoothing out her clothes and taking a deep breath, Yara knew that it was time to face her fears head-on - no matter how daunting the journey ahead might seem.
